extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (examining corps, patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for making and documenting obviousness determinations under 35 U.S.C. 103 in U.S. patent prosecution, including the factual inquiries, search scope, rationales for rejections, applicant reply handling, and consideration of rebuttal evidence. Intended to direct Office personnel how to evaluate and articulate obviousness rejections consistent with KSR and Graham.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The framework for the objective analysis for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 as stated in Graham v. John Deere Co.: (A) Determining the scope and content of the prior art; and (B) Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness is a question of law based on these underlying factual inquiries. Secondary considerations (objective evidence) such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results must be evaluated and their weight determined case-by-case. The Graham factors continue to define the inquiry that controls; they may be reordered as appropriate in any particular case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must obtain a thorough understanding of the invention disclosed and claimed, determine the scope of the claimed invention (broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification), and then determine what to search for and where to search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed (MPEP § 904.02). Prior art may be in the applicant's field or reasonably pertinent (analogous art). Prior art from other fields may be considered when design incentives or market forces would prompt predictable variations (KSR). See MPEP §§ 901–904 for what constitutes prior art and how to search.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for
rubrics_metrics.description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and should also cover the disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching or suggestion to combine, a preferred search will seek references that provide such a teaching or suggestion if they exist. Follow general search guidelines in MPEP § 904 and § 904.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search (analogous art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should follow general search guidelines to determine where to search and may consider prior art either in the field of the applicant's endeavor or reasonably pertinent to the problem the applicant was addressing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art in other fields of endeavor may be used where it would have been predictable to apply a technique across fields (KSR). See MPEP § 2141.01(a) for discussion of analogous and nonanalogous art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences between claimed invention and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use claim interpretation guidance (MPEP § 2111). Consider all claim limitations; the difference between the prior art and claimed invention must be articulated. The mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness (Dann v. Johnston).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness rejection should include, explicitly or implicitly, an indication of the level of ordinary skill. Factors include: (1) type of problems encountered in the art; (2) prior art solutions to those problems; (3) rapidity with which innovations are made; (4) sophistication of the technology; and (5) educational level of active workers in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every factor may not be present; one or more may predominate (In re GPAC). A person of ordinary skill is a hypothetical person presumed to have known the relevant art and is a person of ordinary creativity, not an automaton (KSR). Office personnel may rely on their own technical expertise to describe this level; references that postdate the invention may still be used to show the level of skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel as factfinders — requirement to articulate findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel fulfill the role of factfinder for Graham inquiries; when making an obviousness rejection, ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning the state of the art and the teachings of the references applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings of fact may need to include how a person of ordinary skill would have understood prior art teachings. After articulating findings, provide an explanation supporting the obviousness rejection. 35 U.S.C. 132 requires applicants be notified of reasons for rejection; clear findings and rationales lead to prompt resolutions. Failure to follow guidelines is not appealable, but rejections are appealable based on substantive law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide articulated reasoning (avoid conclusory statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR and In re Kahn require explicit analysis explaining why differences between prior art and claims would have been obvious. Use reasoned explanation that avoids conclusory generalizations; employ common sense but support it with factual findings and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of reasoning that Office personnel may apply to find obviousness, consistent with Graham and KSR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplary rationales include: (A) Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) Use of known technique to improve similar devices, methods, or products in the same way; (D) Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) “Obvious to try” — choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) Known work in one field may prompt predictable variations for other fields; (G) Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references. See MPEP § 2143 and § 2144 for discussion and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of TSM (teaching-suggestion-motivation) and non-TSM rationales
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art and Graham findings justify a TSM rationale, such a rejection should be made; KSR cautions against overly rigid application but recognizes TSM as a valid rationale among others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TSM is one of many valid rationales. The absence of an express suggestion in the record does not preclude use of common sense or other rationales; however, provide a reasoned explanation rather than conclusory statements. See KSR discussion in MPEP § 2141.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Once Office personnel establish Graham factual findings and conclude obviousness, the burden shifts to the applicant to show the Office erred in findings or provide evidence of nonobviousness. 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors and reply to every ground of objection and rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred substantively as to factual findings. Mere statements that the Office has not established a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence will not be substantively adequate. If traverse is ineffective, the examiner may repeat the rejection and make the next Office action final (see MPEP § 706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence submitted by applicants when reevaluating obviousness determinations; rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others) and evidence of unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After presentation of rebuttal evidence, reconsider initial obviousness determination in view of the entire record (see In re Piasecki, In re Eli Lilly). Examples of evidence applicants may submit for combination claims: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (due to technical difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the function each performs separately; (C) the results were unexpected. Review all rejections and proposed rejections to confirm viability; follow MPEP § 706.07(a) when determining finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art available under 35 U.S.C. 102 is available under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103. Admissions and other disclosures may be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of statutory category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is based on the relevant statutory category (e.g., 102(a)(1) or (a)(2) or pre-AIA categories) depending on the reference type and its dates. See MPEP §§ 901–904 and related sections for discussion on what constitutes prior art and how to treat admissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying particular level of skill not necessary when prior art reflects appropriate level
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only facts of record pertaining to level of skill are within the prior art of record, a specific finding of a particular level may not be necessary where the prior art itself reflects an appropriate level of skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held an invention may be held obvious without a separate finding of the level of skill when prior art sufficiently reflects that level (Chore‑Time; Okajima). Nonetheless, ascertain level of skill where necessary to maintain objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertainment of level of ordinary skill is necessary to maintain objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of resolving the level of ordinary skill lies in maintaining objectivity in obviousness inquiries; the examiner must ascertain what would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the time of the invention, not to the inventor, a layman, or geniuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factors (type of problems, prior art solutions, rapidity of innovations, sophistication, education) to define the hypothetical person. Avoid hindsight bias; describe what such a person would have known and been able to do based on documentary prior art, general knowledge, or common sense, and include those factual findings in the record.
